5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • In a recent development, investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • It has been revealed that access is a good thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

In a recent development, investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

It has been revealed that access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely reveals you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s revision calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same manufacturer that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Sources indicate that real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

If the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Recent findings suggest that now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Sources indicate that many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The tech giant running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

Sources indicate that how to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

In a recent development, the lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

According to recent reports, how to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your plan, not the floor under it.

In a recent development, the average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

The Greenwich, a lavish 88-story tower in Fresh York City’s Financial District, landed on the feature as a way to give residents the ultimate luxury—a little more wiggle room in their schedule.

“From the start, we’ve looked for ways to make life easier for our residents and set The Greenwich apart from other condominium buildings,” developer Gregory Davis, Director at Fortress Investment Group, tells Realtor.com®.

It has been revealed that “When we thought about who our residents would be and how they live, time stood out as the ultimate luxury. An in-building beauty room offering nail and hair services was a natural fit,” Davis continues.

It has been revealed that residents reportedly book the salon’s services weekly, with benefits ranging from quick touch-ups for meetings to full glam ahead of a gala or special occasion. The building leverages a concierge partner, LIVunLtd, to make sure scheduling is a breeze.

“It’s a popular and convenient amenity, particularly for those who appreciate having access to beauty and wellness services without leaving the building,” Davis adds.

An extra perk? The salon sits on the 86th floor, 800 feet above the city, so residents can enjoy stellar views while they get primped.

It has been revealed that at The Greenwich, the salon is exclusively accessible to residents. The space also includes two private treatment rooms that can accommodate services such as esthetics and massage therapy.

The amenity doesn’t function exactly like a typical salon. Residents can reserve the space, or a treatment room, at no added cost and bring in their own preferred stylists. But for those who don’t have a makeup artist on speed dial, the aforementioned concierge partner can be used to book professionals through a “curated network of independent beauty and wellness providers with a range of specialities.”.

This approach seems to be preferred over having a dedicated glam squad on staff.

“Our residents are sophisticated New Yorkers who travel frequently and are often very familiar with the latest beauty and wellness trends,” Davis adds. “Many have specific preferences, whether that means organic products, a stylist experienced with extensions, or a technician specializing in Russian manicures.”.

According to recent reports, “It’s not simply about booking a manicure,” he continues. “It’s about understanding what someone is looking for and finding the right professional to deliver it. When residents aren’t quite sure what they want, we’re happy to make recommendations and introduce them to providers they might not otherwise discover.”.

On that note, pricing is dependent on the provider and service.

So far, manicures, pedicures, and blowouts have been the most popular uses of the salon. Residents have also booked the treatment rooms for lash technicians and estheticians who offer facials.

Soon, residents will be able to easily access cosmetic injectables.

“We’re presently developing a partnership with Bel Angé Medical Spa in Tribeca to bring a Botox pop-up experience directly to the building,” Davis reveals.

In a recent development, the salon has become a useful spot for the building, which occasionally hosts resident events. In June, a “Sip and Style” party invited those who live in the building to head to the 86th floor for rosé, light bites, and professional dry hair styling.

In a recent development, “We were especially delighted by the lively mix of men and women who attended. It was a lovely opportunity for residents to connect while enjoying something a little different,” Davis claims. “We love being able to bring these kinds of experiences into the building and give residents access to wonderful local partners without ever having to leave home.”.

The Greenwich seems to be ahead of an emerging trend, with a number of upcoming luxury towers looking to offer residents similar amenities, too.

Three upcoming luxury developments in Miami will soon offer salon suites as part of the amenity package, including Bentley Residences, the Perigon Miami Beach, and Fouquet’s Hotel and Residences Miami.

Advertisers get every impression measured by FouAnalytics, humans and bots both counted, and wasted spend recovered through fraud0 Google Ads refunds.

UPCOMING YORK and MUNICH , Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- fraud0, the firm behind the AI agent for Google Ads refunds, today announced a further partnership with FouAnalytics, the independent analytics platform for digital ads, websites and mobile apps. This partnership builds on the companies' earlier agreement to offer Google Ads refunds to advertisers. It lets fraud0 customers use FouAnalytics impression-level measurement as their digital media governance system, replacing legacy verification vendors such as DoubleVerify and Integral Ad Science (IAS).

For more than a decade, legacy verification reports have told advertisers that invalid traffic (IVT) was around 1% and that their campaigns were 99% "fraud free." Independent audits have consistently found much higher levels of fraud and waste. Today, even advertisers no longer believe these low IVT numbers from the legacy vendors, and many are looking for an independent way to see what is really happening in their campaigns.

FouAnalytics was built to give them that view. It measures every ad impression and collects 300 to 500 parameters for each one. The platform is deterministic, not probabilistic. It uses red flags to mark automation and blue flags to mark real human interaction, such as mouse movements, scrolling and touch events. Because it positively measures for humans, not just bots, advertisers have two levers to pull. They can cut off sources of fraud (less red, bots) and shift budget toward sites and apps that reach more real people (more blue, humans). FouAnalytics also detects other forms of waste, like ad stacking, pixel stuffing, made-for-advertising (MFA) sites, ad slot refreshing and forced redirects.

According to recent reports, fouAnalytics in-ad tags fire after the ad has rendered, so they record where the ad actually ran, not just what the bid request claimed. This matters because fraudulent sites routinely put reputable domains in their bid requests to win bids. Log-level data repeats those false domains, which lets fraud and MFA sites disappear from reports. FouAnalytics impression-level data indicates where the ads really went. Advertisers can then compare bids won, ads served and ads actually rendered.

According to recent reports, the FouAnalytics dashboard summarizes and labels impression-level data so executives can act on it rapidly, without needing data scientists to process billions of rows of log files. If a third of impressions in a month are marked dark red, advertisers know right away which bad sites and apps to add to block lists. Setup takes minutes -- advertisers just copy and paste FouAnalytics in-ad tags into their DSP or ad server.

The partnership gives advertisers a complete governance loop. FouAnalytics demonstrates them, impression by impression, where their money went and whether real humans saw their ads. fraud0 then analyzes invalid clicks, bots, billing anomalies, overdelivery and traffic outside targeted regions, then builds the evidence and manages refund claims with Google. Approved refunds are credited back to the advertiser's Google Ads account.

Industry observers note that "Legacy verification was designed to reassure advertisers, not to protect them," said Dr. Augustine Fou, founder and CEO of FouAnalytics. "FouAnalytics measures every impression so advertisers can 'see Fou themselves' where their ads went and whether humans saw them. Paired with fraud0's refund capabilities, advertisers can now find the waste and get the money back. That is real governance, not transparency theater.".

"We see far too many bot clicks in display campaigns,just like with other types of campaigns," remarked Tilman Pfeiffer, CEO of fraud0. "Now we can finally give our customers the placement-level data to identify and remove this wasted spend".

Advertisers interested in replacing legacy verification with impression-level governance and automated Google Ads refunds can contact fraud0 or FouAnalytics.

Its privacy-friendly technology helps companies eliminate fraudulent traffic, protect ad spend, and improve marketing performance. More details at www.fraud0.com.

Solana’s tokenized stock market has reached $1.22 billion in circulating value, nearly doubling in less than a month as demand for blockchain-based equities accelerates.

Sources indicate that growth has been driven by platforms including Ondo Finance, xStocks and Backpack Securities, which are bringing exposure to major US companies onto Solana. Apple, Nvidia, Tesla and other household names are increasingly appearing in crypto wallets and decentralized trading platforms.

The expansion is also attracting traditional financial infrastructure. The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana in 2027, potentially opening another route for established securities to enter blockchain markets.

JUST IN: Tokenized equities are now a billion dollar asset class on Solana.$1.22B in circulating value, nearly double where October closed. pic.twitter.com/d7T8UgQIfM.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

Ondo Finance has become one of the biggest contributors to Solana’s tokenized stock market. The platform brought more than 200 tokenized US stocks and ETFs to the network in January, covering companies such as Nvidia, Apple, and Meta.

Industry observers note that its expansion has continued through additional trading and wallet integrations. According to the Solana Foundation’s October ecosystem report, Ondo’s tokenized assets on Solana surpassed $500 million.

Meanwhile, xStocks has accumulated $7.5 billion in trading volume on Solana, while Backpack Securities has processed more than $6 billion in tokenized asset trading volume.

Securitize is also expanding its presence. The tech giant added 13 US equities to its Solana-based offering on November 2, bringing its total catalogue to 25 stocks. Its products include shares in Exxon Mobil, Disney, Salesforce, and GameStop. Unlike purely synthetic products, Securitize says its tokens are backed one-to-one by underlying shares and provide security entitlements with applicable economic and ownership rights.

It has been revealed that the biggest institutional development came on November 12, when DTCC announced looks to connect its Tokenization Service to Solana during the second half of 2027. The integration would allow eligible securities held through its Depository Trust Company subsidiary to become available in tokenized form on Solana.

We are advancing our multi-chain strategy with aims to connect the DTCC Tokenization Service with @solana, expanding network choice for market participants.DTC-tokenized assets are expected to be available on Solana in the second half of 2027. ➡️ https://t.co/OdWc9KDeQS pic.twitter.com/vLTK1291A3.

DTCC is one of the most important pieces of infrastructure in US financial markets. Its subsidiaries processed $4.7 quadrillion in securities transactions during 2025, while its depository provided custody and asset servicing for $114 trillion in securities.

It has been revealed that the initial tokenization service launched on October 28, with support for Canton Network and DTCC’s private Besu network. Solana will become another destination as the company expands its blockchain integrations.

According to recent reports, twenty financial institutions signed agreements to access the service at launch, including JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi, Morgan Stanley and UBS. DTCC says tokenized securities distributed through its service will retain the ownership rights, investor protections and regulatory safeguards associated with traditionally held securities.

In a recent development, this gives Solana a potential connection to established securities infrastructure rather than relying exclusively on crypto-native issuers and trading platforms. But the integration is still planned for 2027.

In a recent development, as of now, the $1.22 billion milestone reflects a relatively small market compared with traditional equities. But the combination of expanding stock offerings, billions in cumulative trading activity, and growing institutional involvement suggests tokenization is becoming a more serious part of Solana’s financial ecosystem.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026.

Solana is attracting billions in tokenized stock trading, but Bitcoin Hyper is betting that the next opportunity lies in bringing Bitcoin liquidity into a faster, more flexible blockchain environment.

It has been revealed that bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 powered by the Solana Virtual Machine (SVM). The architecture aims to combine Bitcoin’s enormous liquidity base with the speed and programmability associated with Solana.

Recent findings suggest that people will be able to bridge BTC into the Layer 2, where they can access faster transactions, decentralized exchanges, staking, and other DeFi applications. Its design also uses zero-knowledge proofs and periodic state commitments to Bitcoin for settlement.

Sources indicate that that combination could open an interesting route for tokenized financial markets. Solana has already demonstrated demand for bringing traditional equities onchain. Bitcoin Hyper is targeting a different pool of capital: Bitcoin holders who want access to applications beyond simply holding BTC.

Industry observers note that the project has already attracted more than $33 million during its presale, while its testnet infrastructure is taking shape. Its wallet, explorer, faucet, and testnet bridge are among the components being rolled out ahead of the next development phase.

Recent findings suggest that the HYPER token presently costs just $0.0136, with presale staking offering an advertised 35% APY. That yield gives early participants another incentive to hold their tokens while the network develops. For comparison, conventional SOL staking yields are considerably lower than that offered by the presale rate. Bitcoin Hyper is using staking rewards to attract early participation before its wider ecosystem goes live.

The fundraising milestone also puts the project on a defined timeline. Bitcoin Hyper’s presale is scheduled to conclude on November 26, leaving buyers with a shrinking window before the next stage.

UPDATED 07:16 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Data center backlash is pushing builders to show communities what they get in return, and public-private partnerships are becoming one answer. As the race for sovereign AI heats up, the question is shifting from where intellectual property lives to where compute runs and who profits from it.

In a recent development, canada offers a sharp test case. A modern data hall employs few people, but its profits can fund the startups and jobs a region needs, according to Sharif Virani (pictured), chief executive officer of SPUR Innovation Center.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s a big misnomer right now in the world that’s kind of landing from previous tech, where people think where your IP is where the wealth creation is going to be,” he stated. “It’s not the case anymore. You have to make sure your inference happens in your country or in your region.”.

Recent findings suggest that virani spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and host Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed sovereign AI, reinvesting data center profits in local entrepreneurs and winning over residents through public-private partnerships. (* Disclosure below.).

SPUR treats its Waterloo, Ontario, site as an innovation campus with an attached data hall rather than a pure data center. The company reinvests about 10 percent of the campus’s data center profits in local entrepreneurs through a venture studio and takes first right of refusal on their office space and compute, Virani explained. Canada’s Dominion List counts more than 500 founders who have left for San Francisco, he noted.

“We have entrepreneurship at an all-time low, productivity at an all-time low [and] GDP in freefall,” he stated. “That’s really the result. We’ve got to reverse that.”.

According to recent reports, one of SPUR’s early investments went to two international students who had full scholarships to the University of Toronto and internships lined up in San Francisco. Instead, they launched a startup called Auditorium AI and hired staff, according to Virani. The model also reaches Main Street, where on-campus hackathons helped a former long-haul trucker build AI software for logistics.

“AI allows these people who know the problem, who have earned the right to solve the problem, to mobilize technology to do it and make the lives of their friends, families and neighbors better,” Virani said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant unveiled Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Industry observers note that several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The tech giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it notes can reach $15,000.

It has been revealed that the announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Recent findings suggest that sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it remarked already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the tech giant.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson stated.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter remarked.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

Recent findings suggest that the new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

Industry observers note that on Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

According to recent reports, on Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Recent findings suggest that compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the problem in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

Recent findings suggest that the dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

It has been revealed that amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS announced aims for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton remarked the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

It has been revealed that the growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

According to recent reports, compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The manufacturer did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

After an key hackathon that demonstrated how AI agents could autonomously perform payments using blockchain, global payments giant Mastercard has spotlighted the XRP Ledger (XRPL).

It has been revealed that 36 hours. 179 hackers. 70 submissions. At the XRP Ledger Hackathon, developers used Mastercard Agent Pay for machines to explore latest possibilities for micropayments and autonomous commerce, including how AI agents can transact within defined spending limits and with verified merchants. See what we learned about the future of agentic commerce: https://t.co/S4NwQxxuRi #AgenticCommerce #DigitalAssets #AI.

In a recent development, global payments giant Mastercard recently posted on X about the outcome of the XRP Ledger Hackathon. In the post, the payments firm detailed that 179 developers submitted 70 projects during the 36-hour event in Manhattan.

The focus of the competition was how to enable AI-powered agents to autonomously execute transactions and micropayments, engage with verified merchants and so forth, all while operating within budgets set by developers.

Recent findings suggest that the hackathon was held as part of the preparations for Ripple’s annual conference called Swell. Mastercard, Amazon Web Services, QuickNode and Ledger supported the event, which had a prize pool of over $40,000.

Mastercard published an official article in which it mentioned the challenge given to developers. They had to build AI agents that could autonomously make payments to verified merchants without human input.

Also, the agents had to operate within a specified budget. They had to settle payments using Ripple’s USD-backed stablecoin called RLUSD. They had to do this on the XRP Ledger.

One of the purposes of the challenge was to showcase how blockchain infrastructure can enable micropayments. This is especially the case for micropayments smaller than one cent.

In the future, these micropayments could be valuable as AI agents start buying computational resources or requesting data from other AI agents and then making payments themselves for digital services.

Mastercard’s vice president of digital assets, Michael Broderick, stressed that the firm's technology called Agent Pay for Machines could enable such payments.

Industry observers note that the project that won the competition is called Wraps. Its creators are Adarsha Mishra and Hrishabh Ayush. Their project dealt with how to secure user privacy in AI-based transactions. Their project demonstrated a method to prove that search logs were not being saved.

One of the most interesting things mentioned in the Mastercard report might be how the XRP Ledger is increasingly being used for payments by machines.

Mastercard mentioned that over 500,000 transactions are being conducted daily on the XRPL by AI agents.

Recent findings suggest that also, it’s reported that Ripple has recorded over 10 million payments using the x402 internet payment protocol on XRPL. This comes less than three months after the protocol crossed the 1 million payment milestone on the network.

Agentic datasets on every listed company in 34 countries: sourced, dated and signed.

It has been revealed that VANCOUVER, BC and LONDON, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Allooloo Technologies Corp. (Allooloo), maker of agentic datasets for capital markets artificial intelligence (AI) agents, today reported 100M AI agent traffic a month. That is 39 calls a second, 3.4 million a day, across getissuer.ai and Issuerwire.ai, running on 24 Microsoft Azure hyperscale locations globally with always-on Amazon Web Services (AWS) redundancy.

Investment banks are not short of AI models. They are short of data an AI agent can use. In a 2026 Teradata study, 77% of technology leaders said 20% or less of their enterprise data is ready for AI agents. Banks are closing that gap on the data they hold, with one governed way in and the source, the date and the owner on every record.

Sources indicate that the data a bank does not hold is the other half. An AI agent working on a security needs the issuer, its disclosures and whether it may be ordered, in every market the bank trades. Allooloo delivers that half agent-ready: 41.9K listed companies in 34 countries, a source and a date on every field, and a signed receipt for every read, over Model Context Protocol (MCP).

Know Your Product (KYP) is the duty to know a security before it is recommended or sold. Allooloo KYP, at getissuer.ai, answers it for the AI agent: who the issuer is, whether it may be ordered, and who it is for. It covers 41.9K listed companies on 79 exchanges in 34 countries.

Issuerwire.ai is the dated disclosure wire: 3.1 million dated disclosures across 34 countries, each with its source.

A Signed Receipt for Every Read.

Every cleared read on Allooloo leaves a signed receipt, the Record of Cleared Orders (RCO): what was read, when, and under which market's rules.

It has been revealed that each market is kept in its own country or region, across 24 Microsoft Azure regions, on one MCP server per market. A second copy of every market is made each night on AWS and locked against deletion for 365 days. Allooloo is a Microsoft AI Cloud Partner.

The products are made around the clock by Allooloo's own team and AI agents, on the Allooloo Algo. AI agents call them around the clock and pay per call, with no seat and no licence.

"Today we are announcing a milestone: 100M AI agent traffic a month," remarked Matthew Keddy, Chief Executive Officer of Allooloo Technologies Corp. "These are the AI agents of capital markets participants, and they want crisp data, five years deep, on 41.9K listed companies across 79 exchanges: sourced, dated and signed. Gain the edge with us.".

In Session and Enterprise Grade.

Allooloo is sold two ways. In session, an AI agent calls Allooloo mid-task and pays as it goes (PayGo) on x402, the open payment standard for AI agents, with no seat and no licence. At enterprise grade, a firm licenses the datasets to design, build and run its own AI agents.

About Allooloo Technologies Corp.

Allooloo Technologies Corp. makes agentic capital markets data products for the AI agents of banks, dealers and issuers. Its products, getissuer.ai and Issuerwire.ai, cover 41.9K listed companies on 79 exchanges in 34 countries, kept across 24 Microsoft Azure regions with on-the-fly redundancy on Amazon Web Services (AWS). The result is always-on agentic datasets: in session for AI lab people, and enterprise grade for customers who design, build and run their own AI agents. Allooloo is headquartered in Vancouver, Canada. Please visit: allooloo.ai.

Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Industry observers note that most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to proposal. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

It has been revealed that for years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

Industry observers note that we eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

It has been revealed that not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Sources indicate that before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

It has been revealed that once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

Industry observers note that “Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

In a recent development, if you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a fresh closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

Industry observers note that there’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened historic doors for blockchain technology adoption in traditional financial markets as it approves exchange and clearinghouse applications for blockchain-based derivatives market infrastructure.

On Nov. 16, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig announced that the commission had given the green light to exchange (designated contract market or DCM) and clearinghouse (derivatives clearing organization or DCO) applications for a company using blockchain technology for the execution and settlement of derivatives contracts.

Recent findings suggest that as per the official statement, Selig considers this a major step forward for U.S. financial markets. He mentioned that blockchain-based market infrastructure is compatible with current U.S. financial regulations.

"This approval makes clear that there is a regulatory path for companies that want to innovate and use blockchain technology to modernize how derivatives are traded and settled,"  he elaborated.

It has been revealed that selig pointed out that the U.S. derivatives markets have seen a number of technological advancements, from physical trading floors to electronic trading platforms.

Now, with blockchain technology, he believes there is an opportunity to further modernize financial market infrastructure without losing regulatory oversight and investor protections.

Notably, there is no technical architecture requirement imposed on derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses under the CFTC's current regulatory framework.

Therefore, firms that leverage blockchain-based networks can apply for regulatory approval under the same set of rules and regulations that apply to traditional financial market participants.

However, Selig also clarified that blockchain adoption is not a license to escape regulatory oversight.

Companies will still need to comply with rules covering anti-money laundering (AML), client protections, market monitoring, risk mitigation and other measures designed to protect the integrity of financial markets.

Simply put, the CFTC is looking to bring blockchain technology into regulated derivatives market infrastructure while maintaining the same standards as traditional financial market participants.

Industry observers note that for some time, the CFTC chairman has been pushing for a scenario where U.S. companies developing emerging financial technologies can operate in the country without having to look to international markets.

The latest developments further reinforce the message that the U.S. is open for business for companies building blockchain-based financial market infrastructure, according to Selig.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 07:55 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

According to recent reports, enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part. Power, cooling and network throughput now decide whether those costly systems produce intelligence or sit idle.

Those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing. Rack densities that once topped out at about 10 kilowatts are now on a path toward a megawatt, a step change that forces enterprises to look both above and below the traditional network, storage and compute layers, according to Jack Hogan (pictured), senior vice president of advanced growth technologies at SHI International Corp.

“When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up. They can go get the GPUs, but they can’t power them. They can’t cool them,” Hogan stated. “These are not cheap systems either. Procuring the infrastructure is just the start.”.

Hogan spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed edge inference and how power, networking, model choice and business outcomes are reshaping the way enterprises build and run AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.).

It has been revealed that the economics of AI infrastructure are shifting along with the hardware. Enterprises once sized deployments by the rack unit or the rack, but entire data centers now operate as a single system with shared memory, and every GPU must be kept fed to justify its cost. That change has altered how SHI measures success, Hogan explained.

“Now we’re talking about row and now data center scale. … We’re measuring that now in megawatts,” Hogan mentioned. “So the megawatt now starts to become a measurement that people start to grasp and understand. How many flops can you get through that megawatt? How fast can you process your tokens?”.

Recent findings suggest that SHI’s role spans the full life cycle of these systems. Drawing on 37 years in the industry, the manufacturer builds customized racks in its integration facilities around the globe and runs pre-site assessments so systems can be powered on as soon as they arrive. In a recent New Jersey project, SHI is hosting and operating the customer’s system in its own data center. Location matters at the edge, too, where workloads such as video input generate data that must be processed in place, Hogan noted.

It has been revealed that “You can’t backhaul that. The networks are not necessarily the right way to move that,” Hogan said. “We’re creating the scenario of both the mega hyperscaler as well as the edge inference and be able to tie those two things together.”.

Busy GPUs are not necessarily productive ones. SHI starts every engagement by asking customers what they are trying to achieve, then works backward to the right model, whether that means frontier intelligence or a small language model running on an edge device. Silicon follows the same logic, with GPUs, newer CPUs, inference-specific chips and neural processing units validated in the tech giant’s AI and Cyber Lab.

According to recent reports, “It’s not about the cost of the token or reducing the number of tokens or even finding cheaper tokens. It’s about optimizing and ensuring that those tokens are turning into business value,” Hogan said.

  • According to recent reports, disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today.
  • Malicious JavaScript code snippets were planted on the websites of 178 organizations.
  • The exploit originated inside Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform, a tool that many large companies use for A/B testing, which means showing customers multiple versions of a page to determine which one is more effective.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Malicious JavaScript code snippets were planted on the websites of 178 organizations.

The exploit originated inside Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform, a tool that many large companies use for A/B testing, which means showing customers multiple versions of a page to determine which one is more effective.

Report URI estimates that on November 16 the code sat in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely snippets it crawled, and the real number is most likely higher.

Among the websites that could become victims of the hack are some of the largest names in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Fox News, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. BleepingComputer confirms that the script loads on many of them.

Essentially, the script's goal was to swap a wallet address on the page for the attacker's one, capture card numbers, take screenshots of pages and more. It was a whole stack of tools used to steal personal data, wallets and other assets.

Industry observers note that according to Report URI, the attacker's wallets received about $7,040 within the first nine hours. That is a drop in the ocean considering the names involved, though the losses from card skimming are unknown. A card skimmer was added later that day, and a hidden iframe tried to load an iOS exploit chain on older iPhones.

Optimizely confirmed that an unauthorized party had exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to certain customer projects. How the flaw worked is yet to be confirmed.

Industry observers note that if successful, it could become one of the largest supply-chain attacks we have ever witnessed. Considering the attack came from a third party, we might see one of the largest service migrations in the world, as none of the third-party services and libraries can be trusted nowadays if used through an API.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain tasks to third-party providers all the time, so witnessing a similar situation in our field is more than a possibility.

Industry observers note that for product owners: stay cautious and rethink the use of services prone to exploits. For users: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

  • Anthropic came through with its initial public offering Thursday, but did it just signal a top in the AI trade?
  • The artificial intelligence model maker’s IPO went almost picture-perfectly, really, producing a 17% pop that wasn’t so high that it left an excessive amount of money on the table but high enough to call it a success.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:00 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.

Anthropic came through with its initial public offering Thursday, but did it just signal a top in the AI trade?

The artificial intelligence model maker’s IPO went almost picture-perfectly, really, producing a 17% pop that wasn’t so high that it left an excessive amount of money on the table but high enough to call it a success. But it seemed to take some of the air out of AI stocks. Continued worries over AI spending and prospects, as well as factors such as a likely interest-rate hike, dragged down the entire market, including other AI names from Google, Microsoft and Meta to AMD, Broadcom and Nvidia. Asian stocks too.

Sources indicate that and on Friday it got even worse, as the Nasdaq crashed 5.6%. Bye-bye, $4 trillion. No doubt Anthropic stock will be at least as volatile as other AI stocks — today it fell 9% — but it can live with that alongside the more than $90 billion now in its bank account. Now all eyes turn to OpenAI, which finds itself chasing after Anthropic in more ways than one, with prepares to go public sometime in next year.

Nvidia posted its usual better-than-expected earnings this week, which didn’t help its stock much but indicates, along with interim CEO Colette Kress’ bullish comments during the earnings call, that it’s going to be fine for some time to come in disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang’s absence.

It has been revealed that meantime, Huang mentioned he’s open to returning — but that’s not only appallingly premature at best, the board appears adamant it’s not going to happen. The supposed friends clamoring for his return are just reinforcing their selfish, clueless nature, the attitude that has plunged tech into such low esteem that auto salespeople and journalists have more tech giant now. Maybe those guys on X (always guys) approve of behavior like this.

What’s with all the outages all over the place? That’s what everyone’s asking, and we looked into what’s behind them all. It doesn’t seem to be the obvious thing — cybersecurity attacks — or really any single cause. Perhaps it’s a lot of 20th century technologies that just aren’t ready for the AI-driven speed of the 21st century, making everything less reliable. Or: All those AI-driven fixes to vulnerabilities are getting done so fast they’re breaking things along the way. Still, is it only a coincidence that the U.S. cyber director just got canned this week?

Palo Alto Networks remains one of the most acquisitive cybersecurity companies out there, once again laying out a tidy sum this week, buying AI startup Applied Compute $4.5 billion. It’s a sure bet consolidation will accelerate as AI enables more and much faster attacks. Indeed, late Friday came a report that an equally acquisitive CrowdStrike is looking to buy Zscaler, which has been a consistent acquirer itself.

Next week’s significant earnings reports include Dell, HP, Nutanix, Workday and Zoom. And then we can all take a brief respite for Thanksgiving before gearing up for AWS re:Invent the following week in Las Vegas, with its blizzard of news. SiliconANGLE, theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with news, analysis and interviews.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:.

Recent spate of outages attributed to technical issues amid accelerated AI bug discovery.

Breaking: A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that while it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it.
  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.
  • In a recent development, sangaré came to the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that while it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he noted.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

In a recent development, sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

It has been revealed that sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” noted Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he stated, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move promptly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

Recent findings suggest that what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he noted.

Sources indicate that but you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Industry observers note that often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré noted. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

Industry observers note that but that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

According to recent reports, and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

In a recent development, house of Stake ratified HSP-029 on Nov. 16, and the proposal lowers the maximum annual issuance of NEAR Protocol from 2.5% to 1.6%. On Tuesday, the price of NEAR dipped to $3.12 in the morning and then went back up to $3.26.

HSP-029 was written by Sal Ternullo, CEO of SVRN, and opened for forum discussion on Oct. 7. The vote closed on Nov. 2, and 99.96% of the veNEAR cast was in favor of the proposal; no veNEAR was cast against it. The Security Council's 14-day window to veto the proposal closed on Nov. 16 with no veto, according to House of Stake.

Sources indicate that this is the second inflation cut for NEAR in just over a year. In October 2025, the maximum issuance was halved from the original 5% to 2.5%, and in September 2026, the realized issuance stood at 2.45%, according to HSP-029.

At 1.6%, NEAR will have "one of the lowest annual issuance rates among major blockchains," House of Stake said.

According to recent reports, according to House of Stake, the reduction will start one quarter after ratification, and validators still have to adopt the protocol upgrade. The issuance cap will reach 1.6% after 24 months.

Ternullo estimated in HSP-029 that NEAR will avoid issuing 11.8 million tokens over two years. At the current price, these tokens would be worth around $38.5 million.

The proposal also calculated that the staking yield of NEAR will go down from around 5.27% to around 3.37% if the staking ratio stays the same. More than half of all NEAR is not staked, according to House of Stake.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Georgia-based homebuilder My Home Communities is expanding beyond its home state with latest-home communities planned in South Carolina, Alabama and Northwest Florida, the manufacturer confirmed earlier this week.
  • The privately held builder, founded in 2018, will launch sales this month at Stonebrook in Gaffney, South Carolina, is planning an 89-homesite community in Summerdale, Alabama, and is preparing an initial presence along Hamilton Bridge Road in Milton, Florida.
  • “Georgia has provided an incredible foundation for our company, and we’re excited to take what we’ve built here into newly introduced markets,” said Jacob Prather, president of My Home Communities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Georgia-based homebuilder My Home Communities is expanding beyond its home state with latest-home communities planned in South Carolina, Alabama and Northwest Florida, the manufacturer confirmed earlier this week.

The privately held builder, founded in 2018, will launch sales this month at Stonebrook in Gaffney, South Carolina, is planning an 89-homesite community in Summerdale, Alabama, and is preparing an initial presence along Hamilton Bridge Road in Milton, Florida.

“Georgia has provided an incredible foundation for our company, and we’re excited to take what we’ve built here into newly introduced markets,” said Jacob Prather, president of My Home Communities. “Expanding into South Carolina, Alabama and Florida is about building relationships, creating new opportunities for homebuyers and establishing My Home Communities as a recognized homebuilding brand throughout the Southeast.”.

My Home Communities focused its first eight years on establishing a footprint across metro Atlanta and other Georgia markets, offering single-family homes and communities targeted to a wide range of buyers.

The firm said continued investment in Georgia remains a core part of its strategy even as it exports its building processes and customer service model to other Southeast states.

The expansion is being supported by the Tamra Wade Team, backed by RE/MAX TRU, which is leading sales and marketing efforts for My Home Communities in the upcoming markets. The team has worked with the builder for several years in Georgia, providing continuity as the organization introduces its brand to buyers outside the state.

In South Carolina, Stonebrook in Gaffney is preparing to launch sales in November 2026, with prices expected to start in the high $200,000s, according to the company. The community is My Home Communities’ first project in South Carolina.

In Alabama, The Retreat in Summerdale is planned as an 89-homesite community. Sales timing has not yet been unveiled. The manufacturer said the project will expand its reach into the Gulf Coast corridor, where new-home demand has been supported by employment growth and relative affordability compared to coastal metros.

In Northwest Florida, My Home Communities plans to start with two homesites along Hamilton Bridge Road in Milton. Additional community details and sales timelines will be released later.

In a recent development, “Our growth is intentional, and we’re focused on finding the right opportunities in markets where we believe our homes and communities will resonate with buyers,” Prather mentioned. “With Stonebrook launching sales this month and additional communities planned in Alabama and Florida, we’re excited to introduce our brand to fresh audiences.”.

The benchmark cryptocurrency has suffered a sharp drop ahead of Anthropic’s upcoming red-hot stock market debut, echoing its 19% plunge in the 50 days leading up to SpaceX’s IPO earlier this year. However, if the historical pattern repeats, Bitcoin could be gearing up for a significant recovery, with a potential rebound toward $90,000 by February now drawing attention.

Strive CEO Matt Cole has observed an interesting historical parallel between Bitcoin’s current price action and its performance ahead of SpaceX’s record-breaking IPO. In the 50 days leading up to SpaceX’s $75 billion public debut on June 12, Bitcoin plunged 19%.

Now, with Anthropic preparing for a potential $64.4 billion IPO next week, BTC has posted a remarkably similar 18% decline over the same period, Cole noted in a post on X.

At press time, Bitcoin was trading at $64,665, according to CoinGecko, extending its recent losses after breaking below the $70,000 mark on November 13. The cryptocurrency continued its downward slide over the weekend, falling beneath $67,000 as bearish pressure intensified.

The Strive chief noted that overlaying the two price movements reveals an almost identical pattern, raising the possibility that Bitcoin could be repeating its pre-SpaceX sell-off ahead of another historic market debut.

Bitcoin extended its decline after SpaceX’s market debut, reaching its lowest point 18 days later before reversing course. The subsequent rally lifted BTC 28% above its IPO-day closing price within 100 days.

“If Anthropic follows the same pattern, most of the drawdown is behind us, and it could reverse rapidly over the next couple of months,” Cole opined.

If history repeats itself, Bitcoin could climb toward $90,000 by late February, Cole suggested.

Binance co-founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao also weighed in on the chart comparison, sharing the analysis on X and describing Cole’s findings as “interesting.”.

However, the historical comparison comes with crucial caveats. Bitcoin’s sell-off ahead of the SpaceX IPO unfolded alongside market concerns over potential BTC sales by Michael Saylor’s Strategy, suggesting that factors beyond the anticipated listing may have contributed to the decline. As a result, attributing the entire downturn to IPO-related sentiment would overlook other pressures weighing on the market at the time.

Ledger, a crypto wallet firm, said it had experienced a security incident related to Optimizely, a third-party service used on its official website, but reassured its owners about the security of their devices and private keys.

In a post, Ledger remarked it was aware of a security incident impacting Optimizely, a third-party service provider used by many other sites as well.

In a recent development, we are aware of a security incident affecting Optimizely, a third-party service used on https://t.co/d2pWxdG49X, alongside numerous other websites. Our team has remediated the issue, and the malicious code is no longer being served through our website. This incident does not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices. Your private keys remain protected by your Ledger device. For more information from Optimizely: https://t.co/CxzmBxYadb.

It has been revealed that website optimization platform Optimizely said it had discovered and contained a security incident affecting some of its Web Experimentation customers on November 16, 2026. Optimizely stated that the vulnerable path has now been blocked, the injected code has been removed, and customers have been contacted directly.

Along these lines, Ledger confirmed that its team had remediated the problem and that the malicious code was no longer being served through its website.

Ledger emphasizes that the incident did not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices and that user private keys remain protected by their Ledger device, thus reassuring customers that the incident had not compromised the core security of its wallet products.

According to recent reports, according to researcher Scott Helme, on November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organizations' websites across several sectors through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform. The websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger, and Peacock.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed, with only 1 of the 188 infected snippets found, down from 169.

The main point is that trusted JavaScript is not always trustworthy. A third-party dependency can exploit a website without ever breaking the website's own code or infrastructure.

#41924. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (821 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that want to price more precisely?
  • When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Recent findings suggest that expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

Recent findings suggest that A sold comp tells us where a buyer noted yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Recent findings suggest that imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

Industry observers note that that’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

Sources indicate that when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Recent findings suggest that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

According to recent reports, this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Recent findings suggest that listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Industry observers note that twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

Latest Update: Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem
